<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|was|6830|wash}}</noinclude>theme ''am'', nor with ''be;'' but it has come to be used to supply the preterit of the verb ''be.'' See ''be''<sup>1</sup>.] A verb-form used to supply the past tense of the verb ''be:'' as, I ''was'', thou ''wast'' or ''wert'', he ''was;'' we, you, or they ''were.'' In the subjunctive, I ''were'', thou ''wert'', he ''were;'' we, you, they ''were'', etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>In war ''was'' never lion raged more fierce,
In peace ''was'' never gentle lamb more mild.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 173.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A scene which I should see
With double joy ''wert'' thou with me.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 55 (song).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nay, nay, God wot, so thou ''wert'' nobly born
Thou hast a pleasant presence.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}}}
{{smaller block|The forms ''wast'' and ''wert'' in the second person singular of the indicative (cf. Icel. ''vert''), and ''wert'' in the second person singular of the subjunctive, are modern, being conformed to the model of ''art''. The older form of the second person singular in both moods is ''were''. The ungrammatical combination ''you was'' became common in the eighteenth century, but is now condemned.}}
{{smaller block|I was sorry ''you was'' disappointed of going to Vallombrosa. ''H. Walpole'', To the Misses Berry, Sept. 25th, 1791.
As I told you when ''you was'' here.
{{right|''Cowper'', To Rev. W. Unwin, June 8, 1780.}}}}

'''wase'''<sup>1</sup> (wāz), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wase'', < MD. ''wase'' = MLG. ''wase'', a bundle, torch, = Icel. ''vasi'' = Sw. Dan. ''vase'', a bundle, sheaf.]   '''1.''' A wisp; a bundle of hay, straw, etc. Also ''waese'', ''weese''.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]—'''2.''' A cushion or pad of straw, etc., worn on the head in order to soften the pressure of a load.   ''Withals.'' [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]—'''3†.''' A torch.

'''wase<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''woose''.

'''wasel†''', ''v. i.''   [ME., < ''wase''<sup>2</sup>, later ''woose''.]   To bemire one’s self; sink in the mire.
{{smaller block|This whit ''waselede'' in the [fen] almost to the ancle.
{{right|''Piers Plowman’s Crede'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 430.}}}}

'''wash''' (wosh), ''v.''   [< ME. ''washen'', ''waschen'', ''weschen'', ''wasshen'', ''wascen'', ''wassen'', ''wesse'' (pret. ''wesh'', ''wesch'', ''wessch'', ''wessh'', ''wosh'', pl. ''weshen'', ''wesshen'', ''wessen'', ''woschen'', pp. ''waschen'', ''iwaschen'', ''iwasche''), < AS. ''wascan'', also ''waxan'' (pret. *''wōsc'' or ''wōx'', pp. ''wascen'', ''wæscen'') = D. ''wasschen'' = OHG. ''wascan'', MHG. ''waschen'', ''weschen'', G. ''waschen'' = Icel. Sw. ''vaska'' = Dan. ''vaske'' (cf. OF. ''gascher'', F. ''gâcher'' = It. ''guazzare'', steep in water, < Teut.); Teut. *''waskan'' or *''waksan'', wash (cf. Skt. √ ''uksh'', sprinkle, wet), perhaps with formative ''-s'' from the √ ''wak'', ''wag'', moisten, or with formative ''-sk'', < √ ''wat'', water, wet (see ''water'', ''wet''<sup>1</sup>). Cf. OIr. ''usce'', Ir. ''uisce'', water (see ''whisky''<sup>1</sup>).]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To apply a liquid, especially water, to for the purpose of cleansing; scrub, scour, or cleanse in or with water or other liquid; free from impurities by ablution: as, to ''wash'' the hands and face; to ''wash'' linen; to ''wash'' the floor; to ''wash'' dishes.
{{smaller block|They ''wesshen'' hym and wyped hym and wonden hym in cloutes.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), ii. 220.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Hir forehed shoon as bright as any day,
So was it ''wasshen'' whan she leet hir werk.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 125.}}}}
{{smaller block|The maiden her-silf ''wosh'' his visage and his nekke, and dried it full softely with a towaile, and than after to the tother twey kynges.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 225.}}}}
{{smaller block|He took water, and ''washed'' his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person.
{{right|Mat. xxvii. 24.}}}}
'''2.''' Hence, to free from ceremonial defilement, or from the stains of guilt, sin, or corruption; purify.
{{smaller block|And thei suffre not the Latynes to syngen at here Awteres: And zif thei done, be ony Aventure, anon thei ''wasschen'' the Awteer with holy Watre.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wash'' me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.
{{right|Ps. li. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' To wet copiously, as with water or other liquid; moisten; cover with moisture.
{{smaller block|<poem>The pride of Italy, that did bestow
On Earth a beauty, ''washt'' by silver Po.</poem>
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She looks as clear
As morning roses newly ''washed'' with dew.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1. 174.}}}}
'''4.''' To lap; lave, as by surrounding water; surround; overflow or dash over or against; sweep, as with flowing water.
{{smaller block|Galatia . . . on the North is ''washed'' with the Euxine Sea the space of two hundred and fiftie miles.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 321.}}}}
'''5.''' To remove by ablution or by the cleansing action of water; dispel by or as by washing: either literally or figuratively: used with ''away'', ''off'', ''out'', etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>Go get some water,
And ''wash'' this filthy witness ''from'' your hand.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 2. 47.}}}}
{{smaller block|Be baptized and ''wash away'' thy sins. {{right|Acts xxii. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wash'' the black ''from'' the Ethiop’s face,
''Wash'' the past ''out'' of man or race!</poem>{{right|''Lowell'', Villa Franca.}}}}
'''6.''' To overwhelm and carry along (in some specified direction) by or as by a rush of water: as, a man ''washed'' overboard; debris ''washed'' up by the storm; roast beef ''washed'' down with ale.
{{smaller block|<poem>These dainties must be ''washd'' downe well with wine,
With sacke & sugar, egges & muskadine.</poem>{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 87.}}}}
{{smaller block|I don’t want my wreck to be ''washed'' up on one of the beaches in company with devil’s-aprons, bladder-weeds, dead horse-shoes, &c. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Autocrat, vii.}}}}
'''7.''' To cover with a watery or thin coat of color; tint lightly, thinly, or evenly, in water-color, with a pigment so mixed as to be very fluid and rapidly and smoothly applied.—'''8.''' To overlay with a thin coat or deposit of metal: as, to ''wash'' copper or brass with gold.
{{smaller block|Those who were cunning in “the Art of making Black Dogs, which are Shillings, or other pieces of Money made only of Pewter, double ''Wash’d.''”
{{right|''J. Ashton'', Social Life in the Reign of Queen Anne, II. 225.}}}}
'''9.''' In ''mining'', ''metal.'', etc., to separate from the earthy and lighter matters by the action of water: as, to ''wash'' gold; to ''wash'' ores. {{smaller|''Washing'' is a common expression used in the most general way, as nearly an equivalent for ''ore-dressing'', or the separation of ore from the gangue with which it is generally mixed. The term ''washing'' is, however, more especially used to designate the separation of gold from the detrital formation in which it so frequently occurs. The same term is also commonly employed to designate the process of separating coal from various impurities which frequently occur intermingled with it, such as shale, pyrites, argillaceous iron ore, gypsum, etc. The machines by which this is done are called ''coal-washers'', as machines for washing gold are called ''gold-washers''. ''Washing'' is also the term in general use for designating the operation of cleansing the ore when, as is frequently the case, it comes from the mine mixed with clay or dirt (material which cannot properly be called ''gangue''). This is a coarse operation, which is sometimes a necessary preliminary to the operations of sizing and dressing, or concentrating, as sometimes called.—'''To wash one’s hands of.''' See ''hand''.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To perform the act of ablution on one’s own person.
{{smaller block|<poem>I will go ''wash'';
And when my face is fair, you shall perceive
Whether I blush or no.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 9. 69.}}}}
'''2.''' To cleanse clothes in or with water.
{{smaller block|I keep his house; and I ''wash'', wring, brew, bake, scour, dress meat and drink, make the beds, and do all myself.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 4. 101.}}}}
'''3.''' To stand the operation of washing without being destroyed, spoiled, or injured: said both of fabrics and of dyes: as, a dress that will not ''wash''; colors that do not ''wash'' well.
{{smaller block|I had no idea your mousseline-de-laine would have ''washed'' so well. Why, it looks just out of the shop.
{{right|''C. Reade'', Love me Little, x.}}}}
'''4.''' Hence, to stand being put to the proof; stand the test: prove genuine, reliable, trustworthy, capable, or fit, when submitted to trial. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|He ’s got pluck somewhere in him. That ’s the only thing after all that ’ll ''wash'', ain’t it? {{right|''T. Hughes,'' Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 2.}}}}
'''5.''' To be eroded, as by a stream, by rainfall, etc.
{{smaller block|What kind of grass is best on a hill that ''washes?''
{{right|''Sci. Amer.,'' N. S., LVII. 203.}}}}
'''6.''' To use washes or cosmetics.
{{smaller block|Young Ladies who notoriously ''Wash'' and Paint, though they have naturally good Complexions.
{{right|''Etherege,'' Man of Mode, ii. 1.}}}}
'''7.''' To make a swish, swash, or swirl of the water: as, the shad are ''washing.'' See ''shad-wash.''

'''wash''' (wosh), ''n.''   [< ''wash, v.'']   '''1.''' The act or operation of cleansing by the application of water; a cleansing with water or other liquid: as, to give one’s face a ''wash.''
{{smaller block|Though she may have done a hard day’s ''wash,'' there ’s not a child ill within the street but Alice goes to offer to sit up.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell,'' Mary Barton, 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|A tub and a clothes-horse at the other end of the kitchen indicated an intermittent ''wash'' of small things also going on.
{{right|''George Eliot,'' Middlemarch, iii. 24.}}}}
'''2.''' Articles in the course of being cleansed by washing, or the quantity of clothes or other articles washed on one occasion.
{{smaller block|Military ''washes'' flapped and fluttered on the fences.
{{right|''L. M. Alcott,'' Hospital Sketches, etc., p. 23.}}}}
'''3.''' The flow or sweep of a body of water; the onward rush of water as its billows break upon the shore; the dash or break of waves upon a shore.
{{smaller block|<poem>Katie walks
By the long ''wash'' of Australasian seas.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson,'' The Brook.}}}}
'''4.''' The rough or broken water left behind by a vessel as it moves along: as, the ''wash'' of the steamer nearly filled the boat.—'''5.''' The licking or lapping noise made by rippling water as it comes in contact with a boat, a pier, the strand, or the like; the swish-swash of water disturbed as by wind or by ebb or flow.
{{smaller block|The water ebbs away with a sulky ''wash'' in the hollow places.
{{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Maid of Sker, iii.}}}}
'''6.''' A piece of ground washed by the action of the sea or river, or sometimes overflowed and sometimes left dry; a shallow part of a river or arm of the sea; also, a morass or marsh; a bog; a fen; a quagmire.
{{smaller block|<poem>Half my power this night,
Passing these flats, are taken by the tide;
These Lincoln ''Washes'' have devoured them.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, v. 6. 41.}}}}
'''7.''' Substances collected and deposited by the action of water, such as alluvium.
{{smaller block|The ''wash'' of pastures, fields, commons, and roads, where rainwater hath a long time settled, is of great advantage to all land.
{{right|''Mortimer'', Husbandry.}}}}
{{smaller block|The debris-piles which stretch along the lower slopes of the ranges in the Cordilleran Region are locally known as ''washes.''
{{right|''J. D. Whitney'', Names and Places, p. 125.}}}}
'''8.''' Waste liquor containing the refuse of food, collected from the cleansed dishes, etc., of a kitchen, such as is often given to pigs; swill or swillings.
{{smaller block|<poem>The wretched, bloody, and usurping boar . . .
Swills your warm blood like ''wash.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 2. 9.}}}}
<poem>Wrinkles like troughs, where swine-deformity swills
The tears of perjury, that lie there like ''wash''
Fallen from the slimy and dishonest eye.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Changeling, ii. 1.}}}}

'''9.''' In ''distilling:'' (''a'') The fermented wort, from which the spirit is extracted. {{smaller|The grain ground and infused is called the ''mash'', the decanted liquor is called the ''wort'', and the wort when fermented becomes the ''wash''.}} (''b'') A mixture of dunder, molasses, scummings, and water, used in the West Indies for distillation.   ''Bryan Edwards.''—'''10.''' A liquid used for application to a surface or a body to cleanse it, color it, or the like—especially a thin and watery liquid, as distinguished from one that is glutinous or oily. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A liquid used for toilet purposes, such as a cosmetic, a liquid dentifrice, or a hair-wash.}}

{{smaller block|My eyes are none of the best since I have used the last new ''wash'' of mercury-water.
{{right|''Wycherley'', Love in a Wood, iv. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|It [modesty] renders the face delightfully handsome; is not subject to be rubbed off, and cannot be paralleled by either ''wash'', powder, cosmetic, etc.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 547.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') In ''med.'', a lotion. (''c'') A thin even coating of color spread over a surface, as of a painting. See def. 11.}}

<poem>There is no handsomeness
But has a ''wash'' of pride and luxury.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Nice Valour, iii. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|By this is seene who lives by faith and certain knowledge, and who by credulity and the prevailing opinion of the age; whose vertue is an unchangeable graine, and whose of a slight ''wash''.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''d'') In ''zoöl.'', a light or slight surface-coloration, as if laid over a ground-color; a superficial tone or tinge: as, a frosty ''wash'' over black. (''e'') A thin coat of metal applied to anything for beauty or preservation.}}

'''11.''' In ''water-color painting'', the application of a pigment so mixed as to be in a very fluid condition, or a coat so applied. {{smaller|It is usually a very thin and transparent coat, applied quickly with a large brush, flat and often gradated so as to be darker at one edge than at the opposite edge, or to shade off without mark of separation from one tint into another.}}

'''12.''' The blade of an oar.—'''13.''' A measure of shell-fish; a stamped measure capable of holding 21 quarts and a pint of water.
{{smaller block|“I buy my winks,” said one, “at Billingsgate, at 3''s.'' and 4''s.'' the ''wash.''” A ''wash'' is about a bushel.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 78.}}}}
{{smaller block|Each smack takes about 40 ''wash'' of whelks with her for the voyage.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IX. 256.}}}}

'''14.''' A fictitious kind of sale, disallowed on the stock and other exchanges, in which a broker who has received orders from one person to buy and from another person to sell a particular amount or quantity of some particular stock or commodity simply transfers the stock or commodity from one principal to the other and pockets the difference, instead of executing both orders separately to the best advantage in each case, as is required by the rules of the different exchanges. [Stock-exchange slang.] {{smaller|—'''Black wash.''' See ''black-wash.''—'''Eye-wash,''' collyrium.—'''Rain-wash.''' (''a'') A washing along or away by the force of rain; displacement effected by rainfall.}}
{{smaller block|He was sceptical as to the lacustrine origin of these breccias. Why not subaerial, like those in the interior of Asia?—subangular masses, transported by ''rainwash'' to a distance of 10 or 12 miles.
{{right|''W. L. Blanford'', Quart. Jour. Geol. Soc., XLV, 38.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
